WORKFLOW AND SYSTEM CONTEXT - Parts restore or maintain a parent tool/assembly; exact fitment is a product-evidence question. - Description depth follows functional complexity and evidence, not physical size or price. - Shared buyer priority: exact part identity - Shared buyer priority: replacement function - Shared buyer priority: compatible tool/assembly - Shared buyer priority: size/material when documented - Shared buyer priority: assembly position when documented - Family distinction: A replacement assembly is not the same content class as one of its component parts. - Family distinction: Do not advertise routine hardware as a performance upgrade without evidence. - Do not claim every finisher uses the same sequence; workflows vary by system, crew, compound, and project. - Do not treat compound application, tape embedding, and final finishing as interchangeable operations. - When product evidence does not establish coat stage or workflow position, describe the general domain role without inventing a specific stage. - Trade role: Replaces an individual functional component within a documented drywall tool or assembly. - Workflow stages: service_repair - Typical upstream domains: none - Typical downstream domains: none - System relationship: Belongs to a verified parent tool/assembly relationship. DOMAIN INTELLIGENCE - Primary buyer questions: What component is this? | Which tool/assembly is it documented to fit? | What function/position is documented? - Secondary buyer questions: What size, material, orientation, or included hardware is documented? - Evidence priorities: part identity, compatible tool/assembly, function/position, size/specification, material, part number - Configuration dimensions: part size, orientation/position, target tool/model - Recognize Component function only if present in evidence; general function: Performs a specific documented mechanical, sealing, guiding, cutting, rolling, or control function within the parent tool. - Editorial guidance: Use concise technical copy centered on identity, function, and verified fitment. - Avoid catalog error: Inventing function from a vague part name. - Avoid catalog error: Using another brand’s similar part as compatibility proof. TERMINOLOGY - Use finishing box as the primary neutral term; flat box is a natural contextual synonym when supported by product naming. - Corner finisher and angle head are closely related trade terms, but preserve the manufacturer/product naming and do not assume every corner-finishing head is identical. - Corner roller, corner finisher, corner flusher, corner applicator, and applicator head are related but functionally distinct. - Loading pump and mud pump may be contextual synonyms; mud is acceptable as natural trade language but should not replace exact manufacturer terminology. - Never normalize or rewrite a manufacturer model, series, trademark, SKU, MPN, or part number for stylistic consistency. - Preferred domain terms: replacement component - Contextual synonyms: replacement part - Related but distinct: replacement assembly, commodity hardware - Avoid: universal part without evidence EVIDENCE AND CLAIM DISCIPLINE - Never infer fitment from title similarity alone. - Never turn a generic hardware specification into a universal compatibility claim. - Do not infer compatibility from matching dimensions, names, or appearance alone. - Requires explicit evidence: OEM-equivalent - Requires explicit evidence: improved design - Requires explicit evidence: longer life - Requires explicit evidence: universal compatibility - Claim policy: factual=Use when directly supported by authoritative product evidence. interpretive=Allowed only when it explains the ordinary function of a documented mechanism without adding an unverified outcome. performance=Requires explicit evidence connecting the product or mechanism to the claimed performance result. comparative=Requires a defined comparator and authoritative support for the comparison. quantitative=Requires exact sourced measurements, percentages, rates, counts, or test conditions. superlative=Do not use fastest, best, strongest, lightest, most durable, superior, or equivalent language without explicit authoritative substantiation. warranty_certification=Use only exact current warranty, certification, compliance, or safety language from authoritative evidence. - Evidence is sparse: remain precise and concise; do not compensate with generic domain prose. WORKFLOW AND SYSTEM CONTEXT - Parts restore or maintain a parent tool/assembly; exact fitment is a product-evidence question. - Description depth follows functional complexity and evidence, not physical size or price. - Shared buyer priority: exact part identity - Shared buyer priority: replacement function - Shared buyer priority: compatible tool/assembly - Shared buyer priority: size/material when documented - Shared buyer priority: assembly position when documented - Family distinction: A replacement assembly is not the same content class as one of its component parts. - Family distinction: Do not advertise routine hardware as a performance upgrade without evidence. - Do not claim every finisher uses the same sequence; workflows vary by system, crew, compound, and project. - Do not treat compound application, tape embedding, and final finishing as interchangeable operations. - When product evidence does not establish coat stage or workflow position, describe the general domain role without inventing a specific stage. - Trade role: Replaces an individual functional component within a documented drywall tool or assembly. - Workflow stages: service_repair - Typical upstream domains: none - Typical downstream domains: none - System relationship: Belongs to a verified parent tool/assembly relationship. DOMAIN INTELLIGENCE - Primary buyer questions: What component is this? | Which tool/assembly is it documented to fit? | What function/position is documented? - Secondary buyer questions: What size, material, orientation, or included hardware is documented? - Evidence priorities: part identity, compatible tool/assembly, function/position, size/specification, material, part number - Configuration dimensions: part size, orientation/position, target tool/model - Recognize Component function only if present in evidence; general function: Performs a specific documented mechanical, sealing, guiding, cutting, rolling, or control function within the parent tool. - Editorial guidance: Use concise technical copy centered on identity, function, and verified fitment. - Avoid catalog error: Inventing function from a vague part name. - Avoid catalog error: Using another brand’s similar part as compatibility proof. TERMINOLOGY - Use finishing box as the primary neutral term; flat box is a natural contextual synonym when supported by product naming. - Corner finisher and angle head are closely related trade terms, but preserve the manufacturer/product naming and do not assume every corner-finishing head is identical. - Corner roller, corner finisher, corner flusher, corner applicator, and applicator head are related but functionally distinct. - Loading pump and mud pump may be contextual synonyms; preserve manufacturer terminology in product identity. - Gooseneck and box filler/filler adapter are different loading interfaces and must not be collapsed into one part. - Automatic taper is preferred over informal bazooka in primary retail copy unless the latter is intentionally used as a secondary search synonym. - Use joint compound as the neutral technical term; mud is acceptable as natural trade language but should not replace exact manufacturer terminology. - Never normalize or rewrite a manufacturer model, series, trademark, SKU, MPN, or part number for stylistic consistency. - Preferred domain terms: replacement component - Contextual synonyms: replacement part - Related but distinct: replacement assembly, commodity hardware - Avoid: universal part without evidence EVIDENCE AND CLAIM DISCIPLINE - Never infer fitment from title similarity alone. - Never turn a generic hardware specification into a universal compatibility claim. - Do not infer compatibility from matching dimensions, names, or appearance alone. - Requires explicit evidence: OEM-equivalent - Requires explicit evidence: improved design - Requires explicit evidence: longer life - Requires explicit evidence: universal compatibility - Claim policy: factual=Use when directly supported by authoritative product evidence. interpretive=Allowed only when it explains the ordinary function of a documented mechanism without adding an unverified outcome. performance=Requires explicit evidence connecting the product or mechanism to the claimed performance result. comparative=Requires a defined comparator and authoritative support for the comparison. quantitative=Requires exact sourced measurements, percentages, rates, counts, or test conditions. superlative=Do not use fastest, best, strongest, lightest, most durable, superior, or equivalent language without explicit authoritative substantiation. warranty_certification=Use only exact current warranty, certification, compliance, or safety language from authoritative evidence. SEARCH INTENT - Build search language from exact brand, product type, documented size, model/series, and part identity. - Prefer natural trade queries over keyword repetition. - Use contextual synonyms only when they are technically valid for the domain and do not alter product identity. - For replacement parts, exact SKU/MPN and compatible tool-family intent may be more valuable than broad category language. - For tool sets, search intent should describe verified major tool types or workflow coverage rather than unsupported complete-system claims. - Never introduce an unsupported size, compatibility term, model family, or trademark merely because it is a common search query. - Domain pattern: [brand] [part name] - Domain pattern: [tool model] replacement [part] - Domain pattern: [SKU or MPN] BRAND TERMINOLOGY - Preserve canonical manufacturer spelling in customer-facing product identity. - Preserve trademarked series/mechanism names exactly when they are present in authoritative product evidence. - Do not import a mechanism name from one manufacturer into another manufacturer’s product copy. - Brand registry data governs spelling only; it is not evidence for product specifications, warranty, origin, quality, compatibility, or performance.

WORKFLOW AND SYSTEM CONTEXT - Parts restore or maintain a parent tool/assembly; exact fitment is a product-evidence question. - Description depth follows functional complexity and evidence, not physical size or price. - Shared buyer priority: exact part identity - Shared buyer priority: replacement function - Shared buyer priority: compatible tool/assembly - Shared buyer priority: size/material when documented - Shared buyer priority: assembly position when documented - Family distinction: A replacement assembly is not the same content class as one of its component parts. - Family distinction: Do not advertise routine hardware as a performance upgrade without evidence. - Do not claim every finisher uses the same sequence; workflows vary by system, crew, compound, and project. - Do not treat compound application, tape embedding, and final finishing as interchangeable operations. - When product evidence does not establish coat stage or workflow position, describe the general domain role without inventing a specific stage. - Trade role: Replaces an individual functional component within a documented drywall tool or assembly. - Workflow stages: service_repair - Typical upstream domains: none - Typical downstream domains: none - System relationship: Belongs to a verified parent tool/assembly relationship. DOMAIN INTELLIGENCE - Primary buyer questions: What component is this? | Which tool/assembly is it documented to fit? | What function/position is documented? - Secondary buyer questions: What size, material, orientation, or included hardware is documented? - Evidence priorities: part identity, compatible tool/assembly, function/position, size/specification, material, part number - Configuration dimensions: part size, orientation/position, target tool/model - Recognize Component function only if present in evidence; general function: Performs a specific documented mechanical, sealing, guiding, cutting, rolling, or control function within the parent tool. - Editorial guidance: Use concise technical copy centered on identity, function, and verified fitment. - Avoid catalog error: Inventing function from a vague part name. - Avoid catalog error: Using another brand’s similar part as compatibility proof. TERMINOLOGY - Use finishing box as the primary neutral term; flat box is a natural contextual synonym when supported by product naming. - Corner finisher and angle head are closely related trade terms, but preserve the manufacturer/product naming and do not assume every corner-finishing head is identical. - Corner roller, corner finisher, corner flusher, corner applicator, and applicator head are related but functionally distinct. - Loading pump and mud pump may be contextual synonyms; preserve manufacturer terminology in product identity. - Gooseneck and box filler/filler adapter are different loading interfaces and must not be collapsed into one part. - Automatic taper is preferred over informal bazooka in primary retail copy unless the latter is intentionally used as a secondary search synonym. - Use joint compound as the neutral technical term; mud is acceptable as natural trade language but should not replace exact manufacturer terminology. - Never normalize or rewrite a manufacturer model, series, trademark, SKU, MPN, or part number for stylistic consistency. - Preferred domain terms: replacement component - Contextual synonyms: replacement part - Related but distinct: replacement assembly, commodity hardware - Avoid: universal part without evidence EVIDENCE AND CLAIM DISCIPLINE - Never infer fitment from title similarity alone. - Never turn a generic hardware specification into a universal compatibility claim. - Do not infer compatibility from matching dimensions, names, or appearance alone. - Requires explicit evidence: OEM-equivalent - Requires explicit evidence: improved design - Requires explicit evidence: longer life - Requires explicit evidence: universal compatibility - Claim policy: factual=Use when directly supported by authoritative product evidence. interpretive=Allowed only when it explains the ordinary function of a documented mechanism without adding an unverified outcome. performance=Requires explicit evidence connecting the product or mechanism to the claimed performance result. comparative=Requires a defined comparator and authoritative support for the comparison. quantitative=Requires exact sourced measurements, percentages, rates, counts, or test conditions. superlative=Do not use fastest, best, strongest, lightest, most durable, superior, or equivalent language without explicit authoritative substantiation. warranty_certification=Use only exact current warranty, certification, compliance, or safety language from authoritative evidence. WORKFLOW AND SYSTEM CONTEXT - Parts restore or maintain a parent tool/assembly; exact fitment is a product-evidence question. - Description depth follows functional complexity and evidence, not physical size or price. - Shared buyer priority: exact part identity - Shared buyer priority: replacement function - Shared buyer priority: compatible tool/assembly - Shared buyer priority: size/material when documented - Shared buyer priority: assembly position when documented - Family distinction: A replacement assembly is not the same content class as one of its component parts. - Family distinction: Do not advertise routine hardware as a performance upgrade without evidence. - Do not claim every finisher uses the same sequence; workflows vary by system, crew, compound, and project. - Do not treat compound application, tape embedding, and final finishing as interchangeable operations. - When product evidence does not establish coat stage or workflow position, describe the general domain role without inventing a specific stage. - Trade role: Replaces an individual functional component within a documented drywall tool or assembly. - Workflow stages: service_repair - Typical upstream domains: none - Typical downstream domains: none - System relationship: Belongs to a verified parent tool/assembly relationship. DOMAIN INTELLIGENCE - Primary buyer questions: What component is this? | Which tool/assembly is it documented to fit? | What function/position is documented? - Secondary buyer questions: What size, material, orientation, or included hardware is documented? - Evidence priorities: part identity, compatible tool/assembly, function/position, size/specification, material, part number - Configuration dimensions: part size, orientation/position, target tool/model - Recognize Component function only if present in evidence; general function: Performs a specific documented mechanical, sealing, guiding, cutting, rolling, or control function within the parent tool. - Editorial guidance: Use concise technical copy centered on identity, function, and verified fitment. - Avoid catalog error: Inventing function from a vague part name. - Avoid catalog error: Using another brand’s similar part as compatibility proof. TERMINOLOGY - Use finishing box as the primary neutral term; flat box is a natural contextual synonym when supported by product naming. - Corner finisher and angle head are closely related trade terms, but preserve the manufacturer/product naming and do not assume every corner-finishing head is identical. - Corner roller, corner finisher, corner flusher, corner applicator, and applicator head are related but functionally distinct. - Loading pump and mud pump may be contextual synonyms; mud is acceptable as natural trade language but should not replace exact manufacturer terminology. - Never normalize or rewrite a manufacturer model, series, trademark, SKU, MPN, or part number for stylistic consistency. - Preferred domain terms: replacement component - Contextual synonyms: replacement part - Related but distinct: replacement assembly, commodity hardware - Avoid: universal part without evidence EVIDENCE AND CLAIM DISCIPLINE - Never infer fitment from title similarity alone. - Never turn a generic hardware specification into a universal compatibility claim. - Do not infer compatibility from matching dimensions, names, or appearance alone. - Requires explicit evidence: OEM-equivalent - Requires explicit evidence: improved design - Requires explicit evidence: longer life - Requires explicit evidence: universal compatibility - Claim policy: factual=Use when directly supported by authoritative product evidence. interpretive=Allowed only when it explains the ordinary function of a documented mechanism without adding an unverified outcome. performance=Requires explicit evidence connecting the product or mechanism to the claimed performance result. comparative=Requires a defined comparator and authoritative support for the comparison. quantitative=Requires exact sourced measurements, percentages, rates, counts, or test conditions. superlative=Do not use fastest, best, strongest, lightest, most durable, superior, or equivalent language without explicit authoritative substantiation. warranty_certification=Use only exact current warranty, certification, compliance, or safety language from authoritative evidence. SEARCH INTENT - Build search language from exact brand, product type, documented size, model/series, and part identity. - Prefer natural trade queries over keyword repetition. - Use contextual synonyms only when they are technically valid for the domain and do not alter product identity. - For replacement parts, exact SKU/MPN and compatible tool-family intent may be more valuable than broad category language. - For tool sets, search intent should describe verified major tool types or workflow coverage rather than unsupported complete-system claims. - Never introduce an unsupported size, compatibility term, model family, or trademark merely because it is a common search query. - Domain pattern: [brand] [part name] - Domain pattern: [tool model] replacement [part] - Domain pattern: [SKU or MPN] BRAND TERMINOLOGY - Preserve canonical manufacturer spelling in customer-facing product identity. - Preserve trademarked series/mechanism names exactly when they are present in authoritative product evidence. - Do not import a mechanism name from one manufacturer into another manufacturer’s product copy. - Brand registry data governs spelling only; it is not evidence for product specifications, warranty, origin, quality, compatibility, or performance.

WORKFLOW AND SYSTEM CONTEXT - Parts restore or maintain a parent tool/assembly; exact fitment is a product-evidence question. - Description depth follows functional complexity and evidence, not physical size or price. - Shared buyer priority: exact part identity - Shared buyer priority: replacement function - Shared buyer priority: compatible tool/assembly - Shared buyer priority: size/material when documented - Shared buyer priority: assembly position when documented - Family distinction: A replacement assembly is not the same content class as one of its component parts. - Family distinction: Do not advertise routine hardware as a performance upgrade without evidence. - Do not claim every finisher uses the same sequence; workflows vary by system, crew, compound, and project. - Do not treat compound application, tape embedding, and final finishing as interchangeable operations. - When product evidence does not establish coat stage or workflow position, describe the general domain role without inventing a specific stage. - Trade role: Replaces an individual functional component within a documented drywall tool or assembly. - Workflow stages: service_repair - Typical upstream domains: none - Typical downstream domains: none - System relationship: Belongs to a verified parent tool/assembly relationship. DOMAIN INTELLIGENCE - Primary buyer questions: What component is this? | Which tool/assembly is it documented to fit? | What function/position is documented? - Secondary buyer questions: What size, material, orientation, or included hardware is documented? - Evidence priorities: part identity, compatible tool/assembly, function/position, size/specification, material, part number - Configuration dimensions: part size, orientation/position, target tool/model - Recognize Component function only if present in evidence; general function: Performs a specific documented mechanical, sealing, guiding, cutting, rolling, or control function within the parent tool. - Editorial guidance: Use concise technical copy centered on identity, function, and verified fitment. - Avoid catalog error: Inventing function from a vague part name. - Avoid catalog error: Using another brand’s similar part as compatibility proof. mud is acceptable as natural trade language but should not replace exact manufacturer terminology. - Never normalize or rewrite a manufacturer model, series, trademark, SKU, MPN, or part number for stylistic consistency. - Preferred domain terms: replacement component - Contextual synonyms: replacement part - Related but distinct: replacement assembly, commodity hardware - Avoid: universal part without evidence EVIDENCE AND CLAIM DISCIPLINE - Never infer fitment from title similarity alone. - Never turn a generic hardware specification into a universal compatibility claim. - Do not infer compatibility from matching dimensions, names, or appearance alone. - Requires explicit evidence: OEM-equivalent - Requires explicit evidence: improved design - Requires explicit evidence: longer life - Requires explicit evidence: universal compatibility - Claim policy: factual=Use when directly supported by authoritative product evidence. interpretive=Allowed only when it explains the ordinary function of a documented mechanism without adding an unverified outcome. performance=Requires explicit evidence connecting the product or mechanism to the claimed performance result. comparative=Requires a defined comparator and authoritative support for the comparison. quantitative=Requires exact sourced measurements, percentages, rates, counts, or test conditions. superlative=Do not use fastest, best, strongest, lightest, most durable, superior, or equivalent language without explicit authoritative substantiation. warranty_certification=Use only exact current warranty, certification, compliance, or safety language from authoritative evidence. WORKFLOW AND SYSTEM CONTEXT - Parts restore or maintain a parent tool/assembly; exact fitment is a product-evidence question. - Description depth follows functional complexity and evidence, not physical size or price. - Shared buyer priority: exact part identity - Shared buyer priority: replacement function - Shared buyer priority: compatible tool/assembly - Shared buyer priority: size/material when documented - Shared buyer priority: assembly position when documented - Family distinction: A replacement assembly is not the same content class as one of its component parts. - Family distinction: Do not advertise routine hardware as a performance upgrade without evidence. - Do not claim every finisher uses the same sequence; workflows vary by system, crew, compound, and project. - Do not treat compound application, tape embedding, and final finishing as interchangeable operations. - When product evidence does not establish coat stage or workflow position, describe the general domain role without inventing a specific stage. - Trade role: Replaces an individual functional component within a documented drywall tool or assembly. - Workflow stages: service_repair - Typical upstream domains: none - Typical downstream domains: none - System relationship: Belongs to a verified parent tool/assembly relationship.
